meta.home: I'm Lorenzo. I build software for the parts of a business that are still done by hand. You don't need to arrive with a plan. Tell me what isn't working and we'll work out the rest.
meta.work: Four projects: a travel eSIM, software that watches camera feeds, a product of my own, and a course I wrote. For each one, what the situation was, what I did, and what was hard about it.
meta.about: How I work, what I do before I write any code, and a bit about who I am.

hero.status: Open to a couple of projects
hero.lede: I'm Lorenzo. People come to me when something in the business is slow, gets done twice, or lives in a spreadsheet only one person really understands. You don't need to arrive with a plan for what to build. Working that out is part of the job.

facts.latestValue: AInterest, live and open to anyone

capabilities.title: Six things people usually arrive with.
capabilities.lede: Almost nobody writes to me with a spec. They write with a description of something that isn't working: a process that takes three days when it should take an afternoon, or a number one person retypes into a second system every morning. That's plenty to start from.

manualWork.title: Work your team still does by hand
manualWork.body: The report somebody rebuilds every Monday morning. Numbers copied out of one system and typed into another. It's usually the dullest part of someone's job and the easiest part to hand over to software.

customTool.title: The tool you wish existed
customTool.body: Most businesses do at least one thing in a way no ready-made product covers properly, so it ends up spread across a few spreadsheets, a shared inbox and one person's memory. This is the thing built around how you already work.

ideaToProduct.title: An idea that needs to become a product
ideaToProduct.body: You've got something in your head and no clear picture yet of what it looks like. I've done this with my own product, from the first idea to something anyone can sign up for today. You can go and look at how it turned out.

systemsTalking.title: Tools that don't talk to each other
systemsTalking.body: Your accounting software, whatever the sales team lives in, a supplier's website, something old nobody wants to touch. Getting information to move between them on its own, and getting it right often enough that people stop checking it by hand.

aiWhereItPays.title: AI where it actually saves time
aiWhereItPays.body: I've built AI into a product people use, and I wrote a course on working with these tools. Doing both taught me mostly where they stop being worth the money.

outgrown.title: Something you've outgrown
outgrown.body: It still works, but every small change takes weeks, everyone has their own workaround, and nobody wants to be the person who breaks it. Sometimes that's worth repairing and sometimes it's worth starting again. I'll give you my honest read on which.

work.title: Four projects, and the hard part of each.
work.lede: A travel eSIM sold under the FC Barcelona name, software that watches camera feeds for a living, a product of my own, and a course I wrote.
work.pageTitle: Four projects, and the hard part of each.
work.pageLede: Not everything I've made. These four cover the most ground: a product with paying customers, a complicated one I helped shape, one that was entirely mine, and one that isn't software at all.

course.formatValue: Online, recorded, at your own pace
course.lengthValue: Two modules, eleven lessons, about four weeks
course.note: The only thing here that isn't software. It's on the list because explaining something to people who will go and test it that same evening is a different skill from building it.

barcaMobile.summary: A travel eSIM sold under the FC Barcelona name. The product I work on day to day.
barcaMobile.situation: Getting online in another country still means either a bill you find out about afterwards or a queue at an airport shop. Barça Mobile sells mobile data in over 170 countries under a name people already know, which doesn't leave much room for a clumsy screen. The person using it is usually standing in a terminal with no signal yet.
barcaMobile.contribution: I'm a senior engineer on the team that builds it, and I work across the product rather than one corner of it. The app people manage their plan in, the site where they choose one, and the parts behind both. In practice that means picking a destination, buying a plan, getting the eSIM onto the phone and checking how much data is left. Those are the moments where somebody either gets connected or gives up and walks to a shop.
barcaMobile.challenge: Installing an eSIM is the step that doesn't forgive you. It happens once, on a phone the person has never set up this way, usually on borrowed airport wifi, and if it goes wrong they don't try again. So most of the care goes into a handful of screens where things can fail quietly, and into being sure a change hasn't broken anything for the people already using it.
barcaMobile.proof: I spend my working week inside a real product with paying customers and a brand attached to it. That's a different discipline from building something and moving on. Release after release, other people's code, decisions you have to defend, and problems that turn up long after you thought you'd finished.
barcaMobile.role: Senior software engineer on the product team, across the app, the site and what sits behind them.

examin.summary: Software that watches camera feeds and tells people what just happened.
examin.situation: Plenty of businesses have cameras everywhere and nobody with the time to watch them. A cracked solar panel or a pallet left where it shouldn't be is already on camera, and it gets noticed hours later if it gets noticed at all. Examin uses cameras a company already owns to say what happened while it's still happening, across jobs as different as inspecting solar farms and reading number plates.
examin.contribution: I was brought in to build the product. That covers everything the person on shift touches: the live views, the alerts, the evidence attached to each one, the settings that decide what's worth interrupting somebody for. It also covers the work underneath that keeps all of it connected to the cameras and the detections coming out of them. There was no finished specification, so I was part of deciding what the product should be.
examin.challenge: Restraint. Software like this can flag almost anything, and an alert nobody trusts is worse than no alert, because people mute it inside a week. So a lot of the work went into what not to show, and into what somebody needs in the one second they spend deciding whether to believe it. The frame itself, the time, how sure the system is. Then making one product cover very different industries without it turning into a settings screen nobody can face.
examin.proof: Somebody handed me a complicated product and let me help decide what it should be. If what you have is a suspicion that something in your process is being missed, and no clear idea what the answer looks like, that's the shape of problem I'm used to.
examin.role: Brought in as the developer: the product people use, the parts behind it, and a say in what got built.

ainterest.summary: My own product. Make images with AI, then put them somewhere other people can see them.
ainterest.situation: Nobody asked for this one. Every tool for making images with AI buries the results in a chat window. Whatever you made last week is gone unless you thought to save it, and you never see what anyone else is doing. That felt like the wrong shape for something people mostly do for the pleasure of it.
ainterest.contribution: I built the whole thing and it's live. You describe what you want and you get an image. Everything you make stays in your account, and you can publish any of it to a feed other people browse and search. Accounts, generation, the feed and the bill for keeping it running are all mine. There was no specification, because there was nobody to write one.
ainterest.challenge: Almost none of the difficulty was the AI. Making one image is slow, costs real money every single time, and sometimes simply fails. The app has to be honest about that while you wait without looking broken, and stay quick as the feed fills up. Every wrong decision was one I paid for myself that month.
ainterest.proof: Somebody had to decide what this was, what to leave out, what happens when it fails, and when it was good enough to put a stranger in front of. Here that was all me. Someone has to make those same decisions on your project too.
ainterest.role: Mine, start to finish: the idea, every product decision, the build, and the bills.

aiForFrontend.summary: An online course teaching developers to work with AI properly. I wrote it and I teach it.
aiForFrontend.situation: Developers picked up AI tools in a hurry and started using them by feel. Some of it saves an absurd amount of time. Some of it quietly eats an afternoon and hands you something that looks right and isn't. Nobody was saying plainly where the line falls.
aiForFrontend.contribution: I decided what the course covers, wrote every example and recorded all of it. Two modules and eleven lessons: how these tools actually work and where they mislead you, how to ask for something and get back something usable, and how to use them on real work like someone else's code, finding bugs, tests and documentation. It's published by Itlogia, a licensed online school, and it's available now.
aiForFrontend.challenge: These tools change every few months. Teach the tools and the course is out of date before anyone finishes it, so I taught the habits instead: what to check, what never to trust, where a person still has to think. Working that out meant putting into words what I'd been doing on instinct, which took longer than recording it.
aiForFrontend.proof: You can't hide a vague explanation from people who will go and try it themselves that evening. Writing the course made me put a line on paper about where these tools stop being useful, and that's the same line I use when a client asks whether AI is the answer to their problem.
aiForFrontend.role: Author and instructor. I chose what it covers, wrote the material and recorded every lesson.

process.title: You talk to the person building it.
process.lede: No account manager, and nobody you've never met doing the actual work.

understand.title: Work out the real problem
understand.body: A conversation and a lot of questions about how the work happens now. Quite often what's worth building isn't what was asked for, and it's much cheaper to find that out at the start.

scope.title: Agree the smallest useful version
scope.body: What gets built first, what it costs, and what we're leaving out on purpose. You get all of that in writing before any work starts.

build.title: Build it where you can see it
build.body: You get something you can click through long before it's finished. Changing your mind is cheap early and expensive late, so tell me early.

handOver.title: Hand it over properly
handOver.body: It goes live, it's written down, and it's yours. You shouldn't have to pay me every month for it to keep working. I'm around afterwards if you want me.

aboutTeaser.title: One person, start to finish.
aboutTeaser.body1: I'm Lorenzo. During the week I work as a senior engineer on <barca>Barça Mobile</barca>, and I take on a small number of client projects alongside it. I'm also finishing a master's at the University of Oradea.
aboutTeaser.body2: I've been building software for years and I've worked on every part of it, from the screens people click on to everything running quietly behind them. Picking the tools for that is my job, not something you need an opinion about.
aboutTeaser.body3: So one person holds the whole thing, from the first conversation about what's going wrong to the version your team opens on a Monday morning.

contact.title: Tell me what isn't working.
contact.lede: You don't need a document, a budget, or a clear idea of what to build. A couple of sentences about what's going wrong is plenty. If I think it isn't worth building, or that someone else would do it better, I'll say so.

about.title: The longer version.
about.lede: How I work, how I decide what's worth building, and what I'm like to deal with.
about.intro: I'm Lorenzo. During the week I'm a senior engineer on <barca>Barça Mobile</barca>, and I'm finishing a master's at the University of Oradea.
about.freelance: Alongside that I take on a few client projects and keep my own products running. That's where I try things out before they go anywhere near someone else's business.
about.career: Most of what I've built ended up in front of real people, which teaches you quickly. You find out within a day if something is confusing. I've also looked after the parts nobody ever sees, the ones that decide whether the thing still works at four on a Friday afternoon.
about.interests: The part I like most happens before any of that, sitting with a problem until it's clear what should exist. Plenty of people will build exactly what you describe. That isn't always the useful thing to do.

principles.title: A few things I've settled on.

problem.title: The brief is a guess
problem.body: People ask for solutions, because that's easier than describing a problem. So the first thing I do is work backwards to what's actually wrong, then check that the thing you asked for would fix it.

smallest.title: Start with the smallest useful thing
smallest.body: A small version people are already using tells you more than a big version described in a document. It's also how you avoid paying twice for the wrong thing.

maintainable.title: Someone has to live with this
maintainable.body: Whatever I build has to make sense to whoever looks at it next, and that might well be you. Clever solutions are usually just harder to fix later.

ai.title: AI is a tool, not a plan
ai.body: I use these tools every day and recorded a course on them. That's exactly why I'll say so when the answer to your problem isn't AI at all.

working.title: What working with me usually looks like.
working.intro: The things people tend to want to know before they get in touch.

noSpec.label: You don't have a plan
noSpec.body: That's the normal case. Almost nobody arrives with one. Telling me what's slow, or what keeps going wrong, is a better start than a document guessing at the answer.

notSure.label: Not sure it's software
notSure.body: Sometimes it isn't, and I'll tell you. Changing how something is done, or turning on a setting in software you already pay for, is often the better answer.

tooSmall.label: It feels too small
tooSmall.body: A week of work that takes away something your team does every single day is a good project. I'd take that over a six-month plan that never gets finished.

existing.label: Something already exists
existing.body: I can pick up what's there, finish something that stalled, or work alongside whoever built it. I'd rather not throw away something you've already paid for.

managing.label: You don't want to manage a developer
managing.body: You shouldn't have to. I'll ask when I genuinely need an answer and get on with it the rest of the time, and you'll see where things are without having to chase me.

money.label: Cost and timing
money.body: You get a price and a date before any work starts. If either one is going to move, you hear it from me while there's still time to do something about it.

outro.title: Away from the screen.
outro.body: I read more newsletters than is reasonable, and I spend a lot of my own time building things with no purpose at all. No client, no deadline, nobody waiting for it. That's mostly the point.
